story.headline: Spain stages first general strike in 14 years
story.summary: Spain's unions held a 24-hour general strike over housing and purchasing power before the 29 November snap election.
story.display_body: Spain began its first general strike in 14 years at midnight on Wednesday 11 November, a 24-hour walkout over housing costs and purchasing power less than three weeks before the snap election of Sunday 29 November. The two main unions, UGT and CCOO, reported stoppages of around 90% in the car and port sectors in the first hours, according to their own statement relayed by Al Jazeera. Public transport was disrupted, burning-tyre roadblocks went up in Barcelona, and picketers scuffled with police outside Mercamadrid, the capital's main wholesale market. Average rents in Spain have nearly doubled in ten years. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the election after his minority government failed to pass a housing package. He says the strike is "not against anyone"; business groups call it an election protest, and the conservative Popular Party and Vox have criticised it.
story.why: housing is now the central issue of an election that Al Jazeera says could bring the far right to power, and the strike measures how much pressure the unions can still apply.

story.headline: House Republicans shelve Hegseth impeachment
story.summary: The US House voted 211-204 to refer Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution to committee, effectively killing it.
story.display_body: The US House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday 10 November to send Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Republican-led Judiciary Committee, which in practice ends the effort in this Congress. Massie, a Republican, had warned that referral would kill the resolution, which accuses Hegseth of waging the Iran war without congressional authorisation. Hegseth called the accusations "slander" and "a farce" at his first Pentagon press conference in months; Donald Trump said the effort had "miserably FAILED". Massie said his colleagues "know it's a sinking ship but committed to stay on board". Democrats take control of both chambers in January, and a new attempt is expected then.

story.headline: US soldier held in UK on Russia spying suspicion
story.summary: UK counter-terrorism police arrested a US Army member near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia.
story.display_body: British counter-terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old member of the US Army near Gloucester on Tuesday 10 November on suspicion of offences under the National Security Act 2023, in a case the Metropolitan Police say relates to Russia. Officers searched two locations in Gloucestershire. The Met says the investigation was run with US authorities, the US military and the FBI. FBI Director Kash Patel called the espionage allegations of "utmost concern", and the head of US Army Counterintelligence Command described the suspect as a "senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information". The area is home to Britain's signals-intelligence agency GCHQ in nearby Cheltenham and to a NATO rapid-reaction corps headquarters. The man has not been charged.

story.headline: US indicts three over Iran-linked attack plots
story.summary: An updated Manhattan indictment charges three men with plotting nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities and RAF Fairford.
story.display_body: US prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed an updated indictment on Tuesday 10 November charging three men with plotting nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the US, and on RAF Fairford, a British airbase the US used for strikes on Iran. The defendants are an Iranian-Iraqi dual national, an Iranian and an Iraqi; only the dual national, whom prosecutors describe as a commander of the Iraqi armed group Kata'ib Hizballah, is in custody. Prosecutors say he used coded calls from a US jail to arrange payments to attackers and coordinated with the others in the days before a "major incident" at Fairford in late September. He pleaded not guilty in June. The indictment ties the plots to Iran's Revolutionary Guards; Tehran has denied involvement. The US Attorney's Office's own release could not be fetched.

story.headline: Algeria jails Kamel Daoud in absentia
story.summary: An Oran court sentenced writer Kamel Daoud in absentia to five years over his novel Houris.
story.display_body: A court in Oran sentenced the French-Algerian writer Kamel Daoud in absentia to five years in prison on Tuesday 10 November for invasion of privacy and disclosure of professional secrets over his Goncourt-winning novel "Houris". The complainant, Saâda Arbane, a survivor of the 1990s civil war, says the novel used her story, which reached Daoud through his wife, the psychiatrist Aïcha Dahdouh, who was her doctor. Dahdouh was also convicted; she denies passing on the file and has started divorce proceedings. Daoud calls the verdict the result of years of "violent defamation campaigns" and frames the case as a trial of free expression.
story.why: the sentence lands as France campaigns for another of its nationals jailed in Algeria, the journalist Christophe Gleizes, and will strain relations further.

story.headline: Bern approves TARDOC revision, warns on costs
story.summary: The Federal Council approved the first TARDOC outpatient tariff revision from 2027 but demanded cost neutrality and better pay for primary care.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 11 November approved the first annual revision of the outpatient tariff system (TARDOC and outpatient flat rates) in force since January, but refused some changes and warned doctors, hospitals and insurers that it is preparing to step in on costs. The new tariffs take effect on 1 January 2027 and mainly change paediatrics, hospital emergency services, pathology and several surgical fields. The government has capped the annual rise in total outpatient costs at 4%. It says the tariff partners (FMH, H+ and prio.swiss) have still not submitted a joint plan to keep within that cap "despite repeated requests", so it has told the Interior Department to prepare measures for when the cap is exceeded. It also says the promised upgrade of primary care is not happening: on the partners' own simulations, no primary-care category gains except psychiatry and general practitioners. It wants a binding roadmap with the next request.
story.why: TARDOC replaced TARMED partly to shift money towards family doctors and paediatricians, and the government is now saying in writing that, so far, it has not.

story.headline: Federal Council rejects solar-roof initiative
story.summary: The Federal Council recommends Parliament reject the solar initiative without a counter-proposal.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 11 November recommended that Parliament reject the "solar initiative", which would require suitable roofs, walls, car parks and other structures to carry solar panels, without a counter-proposal. The initiative was filed on 10 December 2025. The government argues that the law already sets ambitious solar targets with large subsidies, and that an obligation would infringe property rights. It says buildings are mainly a cantonal matter. It also argues that a solar push large enough to cover winter demand would produce big summer surpluses and extra grid costs, and it doubts there are enough installers. It says it prefers a mix of hydro, solar, wind, biomass and nuclear. Note the contrast with today's Climate Change Performance Index (below), whose experts list the absence of solar standards for all buildings as a Swiss gap.

story.headline: Status S holders keep free travel
story.summary: The Federal Council sent Parliament a bill keeping permit-free travel abroad for Ukrainians with status S.
story.display_body: Ukrainians with protection status S will keep the right to travel abroad and return without a travel permit, under a bill the Federal Council sent to Parliament on Wednesday 11 November; asylum seekers and provisionally admitted people will face restrictions. Parliament voted in December 2021 to allow such trips only in exceptional cases, but the government never brought those rules into force, because it let Ukrainian refugees travel freely when status S was activated in March 2022. The bill writes that exception into law; it will take effect together with the 2021 rules and lapse when status S is lifted. Stays in Ukraine itself remain limited to 15 days per half-year. Most consultation responses supported keeping the exception.

story.headline: Climate index sees Switzerland missing 2030 goal
story.summary: Switzerland rose to 24th in the CCPI 2027 but experts expect it to miss its 2030 emissions target.
story.display_body: Switzerland rose two places to 24th in the Climate Change Performance Index 2027, presented on Wednesday 11 November at the COP31 climate talks, but the index's experts expect it to miss its 2030 target of halving greenhouse-gas emissions. The index, published by Germanwatch and the NewClimate Institute, rates 64 countries plus the EU on emissions, renewables, energy use and policy. It again leaves the top three places empty because no country is doing enough to meet the Paris goals. Switzerland scores relatively well on emissions and energy use, but its experts criticise thin domestic measures, funding cuts to climate programmes and heavy reliance on offsets bought abroad. They doubt Switzerland can buy enough credits that meet its own legal requirements. They also flag slow electric-car uptake, slow phase-out of gas heating and the country's role as a hub for commodity traders. Switzerland ranks behind France (20th) and ahead of Germany (25th), Austria (33rd) and Italy (41st).

story.headline: Italian top court quashes Schmidheiny conviction
story.summary: Italy's Court of Cassation quashed Stephan Schmidheiny's Eternit asbestos sentence and sent part of the case back to Turin.
story.display_body: Italy's Court of Cassation on the evening of Tuesday 10 November quashed the nine-and-a-half-year sentence handed to Swiss former industrialist Stephan Schmidheiny for negligent homicide in 91 asbestos deaths linked to the Eternit plant at Casale Monferrato. The court ruled that 25 of the deaths are time-barred and sent the remaining roughly 60 back to Turin for a new trial. Schmidheiny, now 79, headed the Swiss Eternit group from 1976 to 1986. His defence argued that personal causation for each victim's illness had not been proven; the court's written reasons are due in a few weeks. No conviction against Schmidheiny has yet survived Italy's top court. Victims' relatives at the hearing called it "a real injustice" and warned that more cases will lapse.

story.headline: Unions push 5,000-franc wage for apprentices
story.summary: The Swiss Trade Union Federation plans an initiative for a 5,000-franc minimum wage for VET certificate holders.
story.display_body: The Swiss Trade Union Federation (SGB/USS) wants a popular initiative guaranteeing a minimum wage of CHF 5,000 a month for anyone who has completed an apprenticeship, Le Temps reported on Wednesday 11 November. The federation says 28% of holders of a federal VET certificate (CFC/EFZ, the standard apprenticeship diploma) earn less than CHF 5,000 gross, and that their inflation-adjusted median wage has fallen 2.1% since 2016. Its congress decides at the end of this week; if approved, signature collection would start next year. The employers' association opposes it, saying vocational training's strength is access and mobility in the labour market, not a state-guaranteed starting wage. A poll commissioned by the unions found 66% in favour.
